risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: A proper randomization method (Excel-generated numbers) was used. No baseline imbalances suggest successful random allocation. Even though allocation concealment was not described, this lack of detail likely poses minimal risk given balanced randomization and complete follow-up.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Although participants and personnel were likely aware of group assignment, this did not appear to influence deviation from protocol. The trial maintained fidelity to the assigned intervention across groups and outcomes were analyzed for all randomized participants.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: All participants were followed up and data on the primary outcome (IAPI incidence) were complete. No indication of missing data or selective reporting.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Validated outcome measure (NPUAP staging) was used. Uniform measurement protocol across groups. Outcome assessors were blinded, ensuring independence. Minimal risk of biased assessment.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Although no pre-specified analysis plan was identified (raising some uncertainty), there is no indication of selective reporting or choosing results based on significance. The outcome measurements and analyses appear predetermined and singular.

risk-of-bias.domain: Overall bias
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: The study is judged to raise some concerns in at least one domain for this result, but not to be at high risk of bias for any domain.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Lack of information about allocation concealment. While baseline balance is adequate and no systematic imbalances are noted, the absence of clear information on both sequence generation and allocation concealment introduces potential risk of selection bias.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: While the intention-to-treat analysis is appropriate, the lack of monitoring or reporting of intervention fidelity/adherence introduces uncertainty about whether actual micromovement was consistently delivered. This could bias results if deviation rates differed between groups.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: The proportion of missing data was small (7%) and was balanced across groups (6 missing in intervention, 5 in control). Reasons were documented and unrelated to the outcome (e.g., excessive bleeding, withdrawal). A small proportion of participants (7%) were excluded post-randomization without clear reasons or imbalance information. Lack of reporting on missingness mechanisms and no supporting analyses limits certainty about potential bias

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: While the measurement method was appropriate and standardized, assessor awareness of group allocation introduces a risk of bias in how outcomes were classified.

risk-of-bias.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
risk-of-bias.support-for-judgement: Absence of a public protocol or analysis plan, and missing detail on pre-specified analytic decisions, raises uncertainty over selective reporting. Only one primary outcome is reported with no evidence of alternative analyses or selective selection.
